name: The Basic Reproduction Number
statement: One infected person spreads a disease to this many others in a fully susceptible population.
statementAccent: this many others in a fully susceptible population
meaning: The basic reproduction number, written R-nought, is the expected number of secondary cases produced by a single infected individual in a population where everyone is susceptible. It is the central quantity of epidemiology for gauging how contagious an infection is. If R-nought exceeds one, each case leads on average to more than one further case and the infection can grow into an epidemic; if it is below one, the chain of transmission peters out and the outbreak dies away; a value of exactly one marks the threshold between growth and decline. Measles, among the most contagious diseases, has an R-nought around twelve to eighteen, while seasonal influenza sits near one to two. R-nought also sets the herd immunity threshold and frames the whole mathematical study of epidemics.
mechanism: R-nought combines three factors: how likely transmission is per contact, how many contacts an infected person has per unit time, and how long they remain infectious. Multiplying these gives the average number of new infections one case seeds when everyone around is susceptible. Because the population is assumed fully susceptible, R-nought is a starting condition; as immunity builds through infection or vaccination, the relevant quantity becomes the effective reproduction number, which equals R-nought times the fraction still susceptible and changes over time as immunity and interventions alter transmission. This is why R-nought is not a fixed biological constant of a pathogen but depends on behaviour, contact patterns, and setting, and is usually estimated from models and reported as a range rather than a single exact figure.

examples.text: Measles has an R-nought of roughly twelve to eighteen, so one case can seed a dozen or more in a susceptible group, demanding very high vaccination coverage to control.
An infection grows when R-nought is above one and fades when it is below one, so pushing the effective reproduction number under one is the goal of control measures.
The fraction of a population that must be immune to stop sustained spread is one minus one over R-nought, so a higher R-nought demands a higher immune fraction.

variants.name: The effective reproduction number
variants.text: The time-varying count of secondary cases in a population that is not fully susceptible, equal to R-nought times the susceptible fraction, reduced by immunity and interventions.

variants.name: The herd immunity threshold
variants.text: The proportion that must be immune, one minus one over R-nought, above which an infection cannot sustain itself in the population.

whyItMatters: The basic reproduction number is the headline measure of how contagious an infection is and the organising quantity of infectious-disease epidemiology. Its threshold at one tells whether an outbreak will grow or fade, and it sets the herd immunity threshold that determines how much of a population must be vaccinated to halt spread. During epidemics like COVID-19 it became a household term, guiding public-health decisions and communication. Because it distils transmissibility, contact, and infectious duration into one number, R-nought lets scientists compare diseases, plan vaccination campaigns, and model the likely course of an epidemic, making it indispensable to public health.

working.text: treat R-nought as the average secondary cases per infection in a fully susceptible population, larger meaning more contagious.
expect growth when the effective reproduction number is above one and decline when below, and aim interventions at pushing it under one.
compute the herd immunity threshold as one minus one over R-nought to find the immune fraction needed to stop sustained spread.

limits: R-nought is not a fixed biological constant of a pathogen; it depends on transmissibility, contact rates, and infectious duration, so it varies by population, place, and behaviour, and interventions can change it. It measures contagiousness, not severity, so a high R-nought says nothing about how deadly a disease is. By itself it does not give the speed of spread, which also needs the generation time between successive cases. And R-nought is usually estimated from mathematical models whose assumptions differ, so published values are ranges, not precise figures, and can shift as data and models improve.
misreadings: R-nought is not an intrinsic constant of a virus; the same pathogen has different values in different populations and can be lowered by distancing and vaccination, so quoting a single universal number is misleading. It does not measure how dangerous or deadly a disease is, only how readily it spreads. And a given R-nought does not by itself say how fast an epidemic moves; that depends on the generation time, so two diseases with the same R-nought can spread at very different speeds.
origin: Rooted in early demography through Alfred Lotka and others, and first applied to epidemiology by George Macdonald in his 1952 malaria models; now the central quantity for describing the transmissibility of infectious diseases.

sources.text: Basic reproduction number, Wikipedia. — the definition, the threshold at one, the herd immunity formula one minus one over R-nought, the measles range, and the effective reproduction number.
